knowledge_point.title: Determining an Amount at an Overflow Point

question.:question/problem: A dye mixing tank at a textile factory can hold up to $406\,\text{gal}$ of liquid. Initially, it contains $105\,\text{gal}$ of solution with $42\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved dye. A more concentrated dye solution with concentration $0.8\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the tank at a rate of $21\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $14\,\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of dye in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since $Q$ is the amount of dye in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which dye enters the tank minus the rate at which dye leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which dye enters the tank.

First, note that a solution containing $0.8\,\text{lb/gal}$ of dye enters the tank at a rate of $21\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *dye* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.8\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (21\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.8\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (21\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =16.8\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which dye exits the tank.

To find the rate at which dye leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $105\,\text{gal}$ of liquid; solution enters at $21\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $14\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of liquid in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=105+21t-14t=7(15+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of dye in the tank, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{7(15+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $14\,\text{gal/min},$ *dye* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(14\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{7(15+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(14\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{7(15+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{14Q}{7(15+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{15+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =16.8-\frac{2Q}{15+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{15+t}\,Q=16.8.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(15+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|15+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(15+t)^{2}} \\  & =(15+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(15+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(15+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{15+t}\,Q) & =(15+t)^{2}\cdot 16.8 \\ (15+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(15+t)Q & =16.8(15+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(15+t)^{2}) & =16.8(15+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(15+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 16.8(15+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(15+t)^{2} & =16.8\cdot \frac{1}{3}(15+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =5.6(15+t)+\frac{C}{(15+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $42\,\text{lb}$ of dye. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=42,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =42 \\ 5.6(15+0)+\frac{C}{(15+0)^{2}} & =42 \\ 84+\frac{C}{(15)^{2}} & =42 \\ \frac{C}{(15)^{2}} & =-42 \\ C & =-42(15)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =5.6(15+t)-\frac{42(15)^{2}}{(15+t)^{2}} \\  & =5.6(15+t)-42{\left(\frac{15}{15+t}\right)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $406\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=406$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =406 \\ 105+21{t}_{o}-14{t}_{o} & =406 \\ 105+7{t}_{o} & =406 \\ 7{t}_{o} & =301 \\ {t}_{o} & =43\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of dye in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(43) & =5.6(15+43)-42{\left(\frac{15}{15+43}\right)}^{2} \\  & =324.8-42{\left(\frac{15}{58}\right)}^{2} \\  & ≈322.0\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: 0 <= t <= overflow onset; capacity > initial volume, inflow > outflow, incoming concentration > initial concentration

question.:question/problem: A flavoring tank at a beverage factory can hold up to $750\,\text{gal}$ of liquid. Initially, it contains $300\,\text{gal}$ of flavoring solution with $200\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved flavoring. A more concentrated solution with concentration $1.0\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the tank at a rate of $30\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $20\,\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of flavoring in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since $Q$ is the amount of flavoring in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which flavoring enters the tank minus the rate at which flavoring leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which flavoring enters the tank.

First, note that a solution containing $1.0\,\text{lb/gal}$ of flavoring enters the tank at a rate of $30\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *flavoring* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(1.0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (30\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(1.0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (30\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =30\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which flavoring exits the tank.

To find the rate at which flavoring leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of solution in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $300\,\text{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $30\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $20\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=300+30t-20t=10(30+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of flavoring in the tank, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{10(30+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $20\,\text{gal/min},$ *flavoring* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(20\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{10(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(20\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{10(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{20Q}{10(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{30+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =30-\frac{2Q}{30+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{30+t}\,Q=30.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(30+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|30+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(30+t)^{2}} \\  & =(30+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(30+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(30+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{30+t}\,Q) & =(30+t)^{2}\cdot 30 \\ (30+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(30+t)Q & =30(30+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(30+t)^{2}) & =30(30+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(30+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 30(30+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(30+t)^{2} & =30\cdot \frac{1}{3}(30+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =10(30+t)+\frac{C}{(30+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $200\,\text{lb}$ of flavoring. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=200,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =200 \\ 10(30+0)+\frac{C}{(30+0)^{2}} & =200 \\ 300+\frac{C}{(30)^{2}} & =200 \\ \frac{C}{{30}^{2}} & =-100 \\ C & =-100(30)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =10(30+t)-\frac{100(30)^{2}}{(30+t)^{2}} \\  & =10(30+t)-100{\left(\frac{30}{30+t}\right)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $750\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=750$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =750 \\ 300+30{t}_{o}-20{t}_{o} & =750 \\ 300+10{t}_{o} & =750 \\ 10{t}_{o} & =450 \\ {t}_{o} & =45\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of flavoring in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(45) & =10(30+45)-100{\left(\frac{30}{30+45}\right)}^{2} \\  & =750-100{\left(\frac{30}{75}\right)}^{2} \\  & ≈734.0\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: 0 <= t <= overflow onset; capacity > initial volume, inflow > outflow, incoming concentration > initial concentration
